title: Step 1: the horizon sets the equity range
objectives: Give the illustrative equity range for each horizon band.
Explain why the horizon, not the product, comes first.
body_md:
Start from the horizon, adjust for the risk profile, then pick products. Never start from the product.

## The ranges

| Time to goal | Illustrative equity range | The rest in |
|---|---|---|
| Under 1 year | 0% | Liquid, overnight or money-market funds |
| 1–3 years | 0–20% | Short-duration debt, arbitrage funds |
| 3–5 years | 20–50% | Debt funds, some gold |
| 5–7 years | 40–65% | Debt and gold |
| 7+ years | 60–80% | Debt and gold as stabilisers |

## Why the horizon decides

Equity needs time to recover from its falls. The shorter the horizon, the less room there is for that recovery, so the smaller the equity share. This is arithmetic, not opinion, and it is why the product choice comes third rather than first.

The ranges are illustrative, not recommendations. The risk profile picks the point inside the range.
example: A goal in 18 months lands in the 1–3 year band: at most 20% equity, with the rest in short-duration debt. A 20-year retirement goal lands in the 7+ band: 60–80% equity, with debt and gold as stabilisers.
say: The horizon sets the range for equity; the risk profile picks the point inside it.
Money needed within a year carries no equity.
never: Let's start with this new fund and see where it fits.
Two years is long enough for equity to recover.

check.q: Money needed within a year should be in…
check.why: Under a year means no equity: liquid, overnight or money-market funds.

check.q: What is the illustrative equity range for a 7+ year goal?
check.why: Seven years or more: 60–80% equity, with debt and gold as stabilisers.

check.q: Why does the horizon set the range before the risk profile?
o: Because equity needs time to recover from falls, so short horizons cannot carry much of it
